note: One thing to research for each president: one major act or event, worded from the pages listed under each item, read Nov 7, 2026. 'for' and 'against' say what each side argued, as those pages state it; 'for_label' and 'against_label' replace the usual headings where the sides are not simply for and against. 'none' means nothing major is listed for that presidency. 'pending' means the sources are not checked yet, and the item is not shown. Office of the Historian milestone essays are marked retired by the State Department but are still published.

george-washington.when: Signed November 19, 1794. Approved by the Senate June 24, 1795.
george-washington.what: Representatives of the United States and Great Britain signed the treaty to settle issues left over between the two countries. It passed the Senate on a 20 to 10 vote.
george-washington.for: Washington put the treaty into effect in the face of popular disapproval, seeing it as the price of peace with Great Britain. It gave the young country time to consolidate and rearm.
george-washington.against: The treaty was very unpopular. Democratic-Republicans said it broke the spirit of neutrality and the 1778 treaty with France, and many southerners felt their interests were not as well represented as northerners'.
sources: Office of the Historian, U.S. State Department: John Jay's Treaty
Miller Center, University of Virginia: Washington, foreign affairs

john-adams.what: A Federalist Congress passed four laws and Adams signed them. They raised the wait for citizenship from 5 to 14 years, let the president deport non-citizens, and made it a crime to publish "false, scandalous, and malicious writing" about the government.
john-adams.for: Federalists said criticism of their policies by Democratic-Republicans was disloyal, and feared that non-citizens living in the country would side with France in a war.
john-adams.against: Jefferson and Madison wrote the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions, which called the acts void. The only journalists prosecuted under the Sedition Act were editors of Democratic-Republican newspapers.
sources: National Archives: Alien and Sedition Acts (1798)

thomas-jefferson.what: The United States bought about 530 million acres from France for $15 million. Congress approved the purchase five months after the fact.
thomas-jefferson.for: The West was elated. Jefferson wanted farmers in the Ohio River Valley to have sure access to the Gulf of Mexico.
thomas-jefferson.against: The Constitution says nothing about buying foreign territory, and Jefferson had always argued for following its exact words. He went ahead because of public support and the land's obvious value.
sources: Office of the Historian: Louisiana Purchase, 1803

james-madison.when: Madison asked for war June 1, 1812. The peace treaty was signed at Ghent on December 24, 1814.
james-madison.what: Madison asked Congress to declare war on Great Britain. The House voted for war on June 4 and the Senate on June 17, 1812.
james-madison.for: Madison and the "War Hawks" called it a second war of independence. They pointed to the British seizing sailors from American ships, arming Native nations that attacked settlers, and blocking American trade.
james-madison.against: Federalists said the government favored France. New England states seldom sent their share of militia, and some New England Federalists talked about leaving the Union.
sources: Office of the Historian: The War of 1812, 1812 to 1815

james-monroe.when: December 2, 1823, in Monroe's annual message to Congress.
james-monroe.what: Monroe said the Americas and Europe were separate spheres: no new European colonies in the Americas, and no European meddling in the new republics. The United States would stay out of Europe's affairs.
james-monroe.for: Monroe saw the United States as a model and protector for the new Latin American republics. Americans generally objected to European colonies in the New World.
james-monroe.against: Other nations in the Americas have not always welcomed the United States speaking for the hemisphere.
sources: Office of the Historian: Monroe Doctrine, 1823

john-quincy-adams.pending: Tariff of 1828: no page read yet

andrew-jackson.what: The law let the president negotiate treaties to move Native nations living east of the Mississippi River to land in the West.
andrew-jackson.for: Jackson called removal "the benevolent policy of the Government" and said it would let the states grow in population, wealth and power.
andrew-jackson.against: The Supreme Court upheld the Cherokee Nation's independence from state law in 1832, and Georgia ignored the ruling. Many Cherokee opposed the removal treaty. About 4,000 of 16,000 Cherokee died on the forced march west that followed.
sources: National Archives: Jackson's message to Congress on Indian removal (1830)

william-henry-harrison.none: Harrison died one month after taking office. Nothing major is listed.

john-tyler.when: Signed March 1, 1845, three days before Tyler left office.
john-tyler.what: After the Senate rejected an annexation treaty, Tyler sent Congress a joint resolution, which needed only a majority in each chamber. It passed, and Tyler signed it.
john-tyler.for: Tyler led the drive, and former President Andrew Jackson publicly backed it.
john-tyler.against: Many Americans were troubled by adding another slave state and upsetting the balance in Congress. Mexico still considered Texas its own and threatened war.

james-k-polk.when: 1846 to 1848. The peace treaty was signed February 2, 1848.
james-k-polk.what: In the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, Mexico gave up land that includes present-day California, Nevada, Utah and New Mexico and accepted the Rio Grande as the Texas border. The United States paid $15 million. The Senate approved the treaty March 10, 1848.
james-k-polk.for: Polk wanted California and a nation reaching the Pacific. Expansionists in his own party pushed for every possible gain, and some called for taking all of Mexico.
james-k-polk.against: Most Whigs opposed the war, and Congressman Abraham Lincoln called it unconstitutional. Many opponents saw it as an attempt to spread slavery into new territory.
sources: National Archives: Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)

zachary-taylor.none: Taylor died in his second year in office. Nothing major is listed for his own presidency; the Compromise of 1850 passed under Millard Fillmore.

millard-fillmore.what: California joined as a free state, Utah and New Mexico became territories, the Texas border was settled, the slave trade ended in the District of Columbia, and a stronger Fugitive Slave Act required the return of people who escaped slavery.
millard-fillmore.for: Fillmore saw the package as cooperation between parties that kept the Union together.
millard-fillmore.against: Northern abolitionists were enraged by the Fugitive Slave Act, and several Northern states passed laws against enforcing it. Southern supporters of slavery disliked the limits on slavery in California and the District of Columbia.

franklin-pierce.what: The law created the Kansas and Nebraska territories and let settlers vote on slavery there. It repealed the Missouri Compromise line that had kept slavery out of those lands.
franklin-pierce.for: Senator Stephen Douglas argued for letting settlers decide, and said repeal was needed to keep the South in the Union. He also wanted a railroad route west from Chicago.
franklin-pierce.against: Opponents of slavery were outraged. The fight broke up the Whig Party, split Northern Democrats, and led to the new Republican Party.

james-buchanan.when: March 6, 1857, two days after Buchanan took office.
james-buchanan.what: The Supreme Court ruled that enslaved people and their descendants were not citizens and could not sue in federal court, and that Congress could not ban slavery in the territories. Buchanan had urged a Northern justice to join the Southern majority.
james-buchanan.for: Most Southerners saw the ruling as proof that they read the Constitution correctly.
james-buchanan.against: Abolitionists were enraged and vowed to disobey it. Republicans rejected any right to take enslaved people into the territories, and Buchanan was blamed for his part.
sources: National Archives: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857)

abraham-lincoln.what: Lincoln declared that all people held as slaves in the states then in rebellion "are, and henceforward shall be free." It did not cover the loyal border states or areas already under Union control, and it let Black men join the Army and Navy.
abraham-lincoln.for: Free Black leaders in the North and Republican senators such as Charles Sumner pushed for it. It added moral force to the Union cause.
abraham-lincoln.against: Peace Democrats opposed any talk of freeing enslaved people. It was issued as a military measure and applied only to the states that had seceded.

andrew-johnson.topic: The first impeachment of a president
andrew-johnson.what: The House impeached Johnson 126 to 47, mainly for firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton against the Tenure of Office Act. The Senate fell one vote short of the two-thirds needed to remove him, 35 to 19.
andrew-johnson.for: Almost all Republicans agreed that Johnson was unfit for office.
andrew-johnson.against: Johnson's lawyers said he fired Stanton to test whether the Tenure of Office Act was constitutional, which was neither a high crime nor a misdemeanor.
sources: Miller Center: Andrew Johnson, domestic affairs

ulysses-s-grant.topic: The Enforcement Acts and the Ku Klux Klan Act
ulysses-s-grant.what: From 1870, Congress passed laws to protect the right to vote, and Grant signed the Ku Klux Klan Act in April 1871. In October 1871 he put nine South Carolina counties under martial law and sent federal troops.
ulysses-s-grant.for: Grant called the Fifteenth Amendment, which protects the vote from race discrimination, "a measure of grander importance than any other one act of the kind." The laws aimed to protect freed people and Republican voters in the South.
ulysses-s-grant.against: When federal troops or laws defended Black Southerners' rights, white critics called Grant a tyrant trampling states' rights.

rutherford-b-hayes.topic: The end of federal troops in the South
rutherford-b-hayes.what: By 1876 only Florida, Louisiana and South Carolina still had Republican state governments. After leading Democrats promised to protect the civil and voting rights of Black and white Republicans, Hayes removed the federal troops in Louisiana and South Carolina.
rutherford-b-hayes.for: Many Republicans, Hayes among them, had concluded that "rule by the bayonet was counterproductive."
rutherford-b-hayes.against: A former attorney general under Grant said Hayes had rewarded "lawlessness by letting the lawless have their way." By 1878 Hayes himself was privately describing violence "of the most atrocious character."

james-a-garfield.topic: His assassination and the jobs fight behind it
james-a-garfield.what: Garfield was shot about one hundred days after he took office and died of the wound. The killer was a disappointed job seeker, and the death pushed Congress to pass the Pendleton Civil Service Act in 1883.
james-a-garfield.for: Garfield named William H. Robertson to run the New York customhouse, a prize federal job.
james-a-garfield.against: New York Senator Roscoe Conkling's "Stalwarts" were outraged, and Conkling and Senator Thomas Platt resigned their seats in protest.

chester-a-arthur.what: The law began hiring by competitive exam for many federal jobs, created the Civil Service Commission, and barred firing covered workers for political reasons.
chester-a-arthur.for: Arthur had become a strong reformer after Garfield's assassination. Republican losses in the 1882 elections also pushed him to sign.
chester-a-arthur.against: A Democratic senator called it a bill to keep Republicans in their jobs. It did not cover people already hired, most federal workers, or any state and city workers.

grover-cleveland.what: About 150,000 railroad workers struck in support of workers at the Pullman railcar company town outside Chicago. Cleveland sent federal troops, over the objection of Illinois Governor John Altgeld.
grover-cleveland.for: Many observers wondered whether the nation was on the brink of "either anarchy or presidential tyranny."
grover-cleveland.against: His handling of the strike turned many Northern workers away from his Democratic Party.

benjamin-harrison.what: The first federal law against monopolies. It outlawed contracts and combinations that restrain trade between the states or with other countries. The Senate passed it 51 to 1 and the House 242 to 0.
benjamin-harrison.for: The law was meant to restore competition.
benjamin-harrison.against: It was loosely worded and did not define "trust," "combination" or "monopoly." In 1895 the Supreme Court narrowed it sharply in United States v. E. C. Knight.

william-mckinley.when: 1898. The Senate approved the peace treaty February 6, 1899.
william-mckinley.what: Congress passed a war resolution April 20, 1898. In the Treaty of Paris, Spain gave up Cuba and gave the United States Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines. The Senate approved it by one vote.
william-mckinley.for: Many Americans were angry after the sinking of the battleship Maine ("Remember the Maine!"), and businesses with interests on the island worried about their investments.
william-mckinley.against: Anti-imperialists, among them William Jennings Bryan, Mark Twain, Andrew Carnegie and former President Benjamin Harrison, said overseas expansion would cost too much and break with the country's isolationism.
sources: Office of the Historian: The Spanish-American War, 1898

theodore-roosevelt.when: Panama declared independence November 3, 1903. The canal was finished in 1914.
theodore-roosevelt.what: After Colombia's congress turned down a U.S. offer, Panama broke away while U.S. warships stood off its coast. A 1903 treaty gave the United States a 10-mile-wide strip for $10 million and $250,000 a year.
theodore-roosevelt.for: At the time the canal was hailed as a major foreign policy achievement and a sign of U.S. technical and economic power.
theodore-roosevelt.against: Colombia had rejected the terms, and U.S. control of the Canal Zone later became a sore point with Panama.
sources: Office of the Historian: Building the Panama Canal, 1903 to 1914

william-howard-taft.when: Passed by Congress July 2, 1909. Ratified February 3, 1913.
william-howard-taft.what: The amendment lets Congress tax incomes "from whatever source derived" without dividing the tax among the states by population.
william-howard-taft.for: Farm groups, Populists, Democrats under William Jennings Bryan and progressive Republicans had long wanted an income tax. Taft pushed the amendment through.
william-howard-taft.against: The National Archives says conservatives proposed the amendment "hoping to kill the idea for good."

woodrow-wilson.what: The law set up regional Reserve Banks under a Federal Reserve Board picked by the president. It is the Federal Reserve that still runs today.
woodrow-wilson.for: Democrats and farmers wanted a more flexible money supply, and after the Panic of 1907 many bankers and businessmen also wanted reform.
woodrow-wilson.against: An earlier banker-backed plan was attacked for giving bankers too much power and the government too little. Members of Congress also objected that the House subcommittee writing the bill did most of its work in secret.
links: The Federal Reserve today: what it legally is
sources: Federal Reserve History: Federal Reserve Act signed

warren-g-harding.what: Interior Secretary Albert Fall secretly let private oil companies drill in the Navy's oil reserves at Teapot Dome, Wyoming, and Elk Hills, California, in return for bribes. Fall was later sent to prison.

calvin-coolidge.what: The law limited each nationality to 2 percent of its number in the 1890 census, which cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe, and it shut out immigrants from Asia.
calvin-coolidge.for: Supporters of limits wanted to preserve what the State Department historian calls "the ideal of U.S. homogeneity."
calvin-coolidge.against: Many in Japan were deeply offended and the Japanese government protested. Others in the United States pushed to raise the quotas.
sources: Office of the Historian: The Immigration Act of 1924

herbert-hoover.what: Congress raised tariffs on farm and factory imports to very high levels, and Hoover signed the bill.
herbert-hoover.for: Senators from industrial states wanted higher tariffs on manufactured imports, and Hoover backed protection for farmers.
herbert-hoover.against: Most economists and historians agree the higher rates did little to help the economy and hurt world trade. Some Democrats said the tariff caused the Great Depression, a charge the Miller Center calls politically motivated and inaccurate.

franklin-d-roosevelt.what: The law created old-age benefits for workers, unemployment insurance, and aid for dependent mothers and children, blind people and people with disabilities.
franklin-d-roosevelt.for: Roosevelt asked Congress for "social security" laws on January 17, 1935, and his allies in both chambers brought bills the same day.
franklin-d-roosevelt.against: Opponents called it government overreach into private life, and some objected to the new taxes on employers.

dwight-d-eisenhower.what: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 set up a 41,000-mile system of interstate highways and authorized $25 billion for fiscal years 1957 to 1969.
dwight-d-eisenhower.for: The law called the system important to national defense. It boosted the economy and made long drives faster and safer.
dwight-d-eisenhower.against: Highways through cities cut through neighborhoods and destroyed housing, much of it in poorer areas, and helped empty out downtowns. Many small towns were bypassed.
sources: National Archives: National Interstate and Defense Highways Act (1956)

john-f-kennedy.what: A U-2 spy plane photographed Soviet missile sites in Cuba on October 14. Kennedy ordered a naval "quarantine" on October 22, and on October 28 Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev said the missiles would be taken out.
john-f-kennedy.for: Kennedy chose the quarantine, a word picked to set it apart legally from a blockade.
john-f-kennedy.against: The Joint Chiefs of Staff and others argued for an air strike followed by an invasion. Part of the deal, removing U.S. missiles from Turkey, was kept secret.
sources: Office of the Historian: The Cuban Missile Crisis, October 1962

lyndon-b-johnson.what: The law outlawed segregation in public places and in businesses such as theaters, restaurants and hotels, banned job discrimination, and created the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission.
lyndon-b-johnson.for: Senator Hubert Humphrey, Johnson and Republican leader Everett Dirksen gathered enough votes from both parties to end the filibuster. The Senate passed it 73 to 27.
lyndon-b-johnson.against: Southern Democrats tried to "talk the bill to death" in a long filibuster.

richard-nixon.what: Five men were arrested inside the Democratic National Committee offices. The cover-up that followed reached the White House. After the Supreme Court ruled 8 to 0 that Nixon must hand over his tapes, he announced his resignation on August 8, 1974, effective at noon the next day.
links: History case: Watergate, with both sides and every source

gerald-r-ford.what: Ford gave Nixon a "full, free, and absolute pardon" for any crimes he committed, or may have committed, as president.
gerald-r-ford.for: Ford said Nixon had suffered enough and that a trial would stir up divisive passions again.
gerald-r-ford.against: Polls showed most Americans wanted Nixon punished. Ford's press secretary resigned in protest and his approval fell from the high sixties to the high thirties. Ford later told Congress, "There was no deal, period."

jimmy-carter.when: September 5 to 17, 1978. The peace treaty was signed March 26, 1979.
jimmy-carter.what: At Camp David, Carter, Egyptian President Anwar Sadat and Israeli Prime Minister Menachem Begin signed two frameworks that led to a peace treaty between Egypt and Israel.
jimmy-carter.for: It broke a long deadlock and set out a path to a detailed Egyptian-Israeli peace agreement and a plan for Palestinian self-government in Gaza and the West Bank.
jimmy-carter.against: Egypt and Israel disagreed over withdrawal to the 1967 borders, and the administration could not win support for the accords from Jordan or Saudi Arabia.
sources: Office of the Historian: The Camp David Accords and the Arab-Israeli peace process

ronald-reagan.what: The Economic Recovery Tax Act cut taxes by 25 percent over three years.
ronald-reagan.for: Supporters credit the 1981 tax cuts for the economic boom that began in 1983. Reagan's supply-side advisers argued that growth would widen the tax base.
ronald-reagan.against: Critics warned that tax cuts, smaller spending cuts and more defense spending together were "a recipe for an unbalanced federal budget and a larger national debt."
links: See the deficit and debt during his budget years, above
sources: Wikipedia: Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (secondary)

george-h-w-bush.what: Iraq invaded Kuwait on August 2, 1990. The UN set a January 15, 1991 deadline, and Congress narrowly voted to authorize force. The air war began in mid-January, the ground war on February 24, and a ceasefire came four days later. 148 U.S. soldiers were killed.
george-h-w-bush.for: The coalition's main goal was to make Iraq leave Kuwait, and it did. The victory also lifted the morale of the U.S. military.
george-h-w-bush.against: Critics said the victory was hollow because Saddam Hussein stayed in power.
sources: Office of the Historian: The Gulf War, 1991
Miller Center: George H. W. Bush, foreign affairs

george-w-bush.when: Signed October 26, 2001, about six weeks after the September 11 attacks.
george-w-bush.what: The law was written in direct response to the attacks. It passed the House 357 to 66 and the Senate 98 to 1.
george-w-bush.for: Its stated goal was to greatly strengthen national security.
george-w-bush.against: Critics objected to holding immigrants indefinitely, searching homes and records without the owner's knowledge, and wider use of national security letters to get business records.
